title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM THOMAS’ DOUBT
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM THOMAS’ DOUBT
There are moments in every believer’s life that never make it into testimonies.
The moments after the worship music stops.
The moments after the church service ends.
The moments when prayers seem to bounce off the ceiling.
The moments when you secretly wonder if God really hears you.
The moments when everyone around you seems certain, while you quietly wrestle with questions you are afraid to speak aloud.
Many Christians know the story of Thomas.
Most remember him by a nickname history gave him: “Doubting Thomas.”
But the more I studied his story, the more I realized something unsettling.
Thomas is not the villain of the story.
Thomas is us.
And perhaps one of the greatest lessons I have ever learned about faith came from the disciple whose name became synonymous with doubt.
His story begins in the shadow of one of the greatest scandals in human history.
Jesus Christ had been crucified.
The Messiah had been publicly humiliated.
The One who healed the sick, opened blind eyes, raised the dead, and preached the Kingdom had been nailed to a Roman cross.
The disciples were shattered.
Their hopes appeared buried in a borrowed tomb.
Then something extraordinary happened.
Jesus rose from the dead.
Yet Thomas was absent during the first appearance.
John records it this way:

“So the other disciples told him, ‘We have seen the Lord.’ But he said to them, ‘Unless I see in His hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into His side, I will never believe.’” (John 20:25)
Many have criticized Thomas.
I used to.
Then I realized something.
Thomas was not demanding more evidence than the other disciples received.
The others had already seen Jesus.
Thomas simply wanted the same encounter they had.
His doubt was not rebellion.
His doubt was wounded disappointment.
There is a difference.
The Greek word translated “believe” here comes from πιστεύω (pisteuō), meaning to trust, rely upon, place confidence in.
Thomas was not merely questioning information.
He was struggling to trust again.
And who among us has not been there?
Perhaps you trusted God for healing.
Perhaps you trusted God to save a marriage.
Perhaps you trusted God for provision.
Perhaps you prayed for someone you loved and still watched them walk away.
Sometimes disappointment creates questions that certainty alone cannot answer.
The deeper the wound, the harder trust becomes.
What amazes me is not Thomas’ doubt.
It is Jesus’ response.
Eight days later, Jesus appeared again.
Notice what He did not do.
He did not shame Thomas.
He did not humiliate him.
He did not publicly expose him.
He did not say, “How dare you question Me?”
Instead, Jesus walked directly toward the doubter.
“Put your finger here, and see My hands; and put out your hand, and place it in My side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.” (John 20:27)
The phrase “do not disbelieve” comes from the Greek μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος (mē ginou apistos).
Literally, it means:
“Stop becoming unbelieving.”
Jesus was not condemning Thomas.
He was rescuing him from settling into unbelief.
There is profound grace in that distinction.
Doubt visits many believers.
Unbelief chooses to stay.
Doubt asks questions.
Unbelief closes its ears.
Doubt seeks truth.
Unbelief rejects it.
Jesus met Thomas in the middle of his struggle and invited him closer.
Not farther away.
How many people today have walked away from Christ because they thought their questions disqualified them?
How many sit silently in church afraid someone will discover they are struggling?
How many feel ashamed because their faith feels weaker than it used to?
Thomas teaches us that honest questions can become doorways to deeper faith when brought before Jesus.
Then comes one of the most beautiful confessions in all of Scripture.
Thomas answered:
“My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28)
In Greek:

Ὁ Κύριός μου καὶ ὁ Θεός μου
(Ho Kyrios mou kai ho Theos mou)
“My Lord and my God.”
This is one of the clearest declarations of Christ’s deity in the entire New Testament.
The doubter became the confessor.
The skeptic became the worshiper.
The man history remembers for questioning became one of the strongest witnesses to the resurrection.
Tradition records that Thomas eventually carried the Gospel as far as India, suffering greatly for the sake of Christ and ultimately dying as a martyr.
The disciple remembered for doubt became a fearless ambassador of faith.
That is what Jesus does.
He rewrites stories.
The world labels people by their worst moments.
Jesus defines them by His grace.
The world says failure.
Jesus says redemption.
The world says scandal.
Jesus says restoration.
The world says doubt.
Jesus says disciple.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The entire Bible is filled with people whose stories should have ended in shame.
Abraham doubted.
Moses hesitated.
David fell.
Peter denied.
Paul persecuted.
Thomas questioned.
Yet Jesus transformed them all.
The Gospel is not a collection of perfect people impressing God.
It is the story of a perfect Savior rescuing imperfect people.
That truth becomes even more powerful when we consider the Hebrew concept of grace.
The Hebrew word חֵן (chen) means favor, grace, acceptance freely given.
Grace is not earned.
Grace is received.
And nowhere is that grace displayed more clearly than at the cross.
When Jesus cried out:
“It is finished.”
The Greek word was τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
A commercial term meaning:
“Paid in full.”
The debt of sin.
The shame of failure.
The burden of guilt.
The weight of condemnation.
Paid in full.
Thomas discovered that the resurrected Christ was greater than his doubts.
And many of us need that reminder today.
Your questions are not stronger than Jesus.
Your fears are not stronger than Jesus.
Your disappointments are not stronger than Jesus.
Your past is not stronger than Jesus.
Your failures are not stronger than Jesus.
Your doubts are not stronger than Jesus.
The scars in Jesus’ hands were enough for Thomas.
They are enough for us.
Because those scars tell a story.
A story of sacrifice.
A story of redemption.
A story of mercy.
A story of grace.
A story that continues rewriting lives today.
Perhaps that is why Thomas’ story resonates so deeply.
Because many of us are not standing on mountaintops of certainty.
We are standing in the tension between faith and fear.
Between trust and disappointment.
Between hope and heartbreak.
And there, in that sacred tension, Jesus still comes near.
Not with condemnation.
Not with ridicule.
Not with shame.
But with grace.
If this article stirred something in your heart, do not let the moment pass.
Most importantly, your support helps advance the mission of proclaiming the Gospel and pointing more people to Jesus.
And if this message met you in a place you rarely talk about, be honest.
Your testimony may be the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because sometimes the strongest faith is not found in people who never questioned.
Sometimes it is found in those who met Jesus on the other side of their questions and discovered He was faithful all along.
The scars that convinced Thomas still testify today.
The risen Christ is not afraid of your questions.
He is inviting you closer.
